## formal
Let $V$ be the span of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ in $\Cl(9,0)$, $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$, and $j(v) = v\cdot J$ the complex structure ($e_{3} \mapsto e_{4}$, $e_{4} \mapsto -e_{3}$, and so on), with $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega = e_{357} - e_{368} - e_{458} - e_{467}$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega = e_{457} + e_{367} + e_{358} - e_{468}$, the real and imaginary parts of the $J$-complex volume form on the frame $e_{3}, e_{5}, e_{7}$. Let $SU(3)$ be the group of rotations of $V$ that commute with $j$ and fix $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ (for a $j$-linear rotation, fixing $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ is unit $J$-determinant), with Haar measure $dU$, and let $G$ be its subset of signed permutations of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$. For a link $U$ write $\mathrm{tr}\,U = \sum_{a}e_{a}\cdot U(e_{a})$ (twice the real part of the $J$-complex trace) and $\chi(U) = \tfrac16\mathrm{tr}\,U$; the lattice weight is $\prod_{p}\exp(\beta\chi(U_{p}))$, $\beta = 6/g^{2}$, as in Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The colour group and a finite subgroup; computed.)} The bivectors of $V$ commuting with $J$ and with $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ form an eight-dimensional Lie algebra orthogonal to $J$, the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}. $G$ is a group of order $96$; each element is $v \mapsto RvR^{-1}$ for a rational even versor $R$ with $RJR^{-1} = J$ and $R\,\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega\,R^{-1} = \mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$. The linear maps of $V$ commuting with $G$ are the span of $1$ and $j$, so $G$ is irreducible on the $J$-complex three-space and its central elements have the form $a + bj$; the only such element of $G$ is $1$, so its centre is trivial. The centre of $SU(3)$ is $\{1, \omega, \omega^{2}\}$, $\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}j$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Equal averages through degree three; proved.)} For $k = 1, 2, 3$ the $G$-invariant subspace of $V^{\otimes k}$ is the $SU(3)$-invariant one: $0$; the span of the metric and the form of $J$; the span of $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$. Hence $\int f(U)\,dU = \tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{g \in G}f(g)$ for every polynomial $f$ of degree at most three in the components of $U$, and, for finitely many independent links, for every polynomial of degree at most three in each link.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Degree four separates them; computed.)} In $V^{\otimes 4}$ the invariants have dimension $12$ for $SU(3)$ and $20$ for $G$. The derivation of $J$ vanishes on the $SU(3)$-invariants and has eigenvalues $\pm 4$ times the unit of $J$ on a two-dimensional part of the $G$-invariants, on which $\omega$ would act by $\omega^{\pm 4} \neq 1$: for the $J$-complex trace $t$, $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}t^{4} = 1$ while $\int t^{4}\,dU = 0$; and $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{4} = 20$ against $\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{4}dU = 12$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Shared strong-coupling data; proved, sampled for the loops.)} For $j$-linear $X$, $Y$, $\int\mathrm{tr}(XU)\,dU = 0$ and $\int\mathrm{tr}(XU)\,\mathrm{tr}(U^{-1}Y)\,dU = \tfrac13\mathrm{tr}(XY)$, and the same over $G$. So every term of the strong-coupling expansion (the expansion of $\prod_{p}\exp(\beta\chi(U_{p}))$ in powers of $\beta$) whose integrand has degree at most three in each link has the same value for $G$ and for $SU(3)$. In particular, for every $R \times T$ rectangular fundamental loop $C$ the term of order $\beta^{RT}$ in $\langle\chi(U_{C})\rangle$ from the $RT$ plaquettes of the rectangle is $(\beta/18)^{RT}$ for both (summed over $G$ for $1 \times 1$ and $2 \times 1$); for $SU(3)$ it is the leading term, by its centre, while for $G$, which has no centre, it is not shown to be leading; and the term of a connected plaquette correlator from a tube of plaquettes joining the two, each to first order, has degree two on every link and agrees.
\item[(v)] \emph{(The plaquette; proved.)} With $z(\beta) = \int\exp(\beta\chi(U))\,dU$ (for $G$, the average over $G$), $(\ln z)'(\beta) = \kappa_{2}\beta + \tfrac12\kappa_{3}\beta^{2} + \tfrac16\kappa_{4}\beta^{3} + O(\beta^{4})$, $\kappa_{n}$ the cumulants of $\chi$: $\tfrac{\beta}{18} + \tfrac{\beta^{2}}{216} + 0\cdot\beta^{3}$ for $SU(3)$ and $\tfrac{\beta}{18} + \tfrac{\beta^{2}}{216} + \tfrac{\beta^{3}}{972}$ for $G$. On the hypercubic lattice of dimension at least three $\langle\chi(U_{p})\rangle = (\ln z)'(\beta) + O(\beta^{5})$ for both, the first closed surface being the boundary of an elementary cube (standard).
\item[(vi)] \emph{(A gapped finite weight; computed.)} $\chi(g) \le \tfrac13$ for every $g \neq 1$ in $G$, while on $SU(3)$ the rational elements $\mathrm{diag}(z, \bar z, 1)$, $z = ((n^{2} - 1) + 2nj)/(n^{2} + 1)$, have $1 - \chi = 4/(3(n^{2} + 1))$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading (argued).} No term of the colour lattice's strong-coupling expansion that uses link moments of degree at most three (the term of every rectangle from its own plaquettes, the plaquette through $\beta^{2}$, and the tube terms of plaquette correlators from which the leading strong-coupling glueball decay rate is read) distinguishes $SU(3)$ from $G$, a finite group without centre whose weight is gapped at the identity, so that its plaquettes freeze at weak coupling and it has no continuum limit. For $G$ a fundamental line can end on sheets through the degree-four invariant of (iii), so its large loops need not follow the rectangle's own term. With the stored comparison with compact $U(1)$ (same form, \claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(vi); deconfined and massless at weak coupling, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(iv)), strong-coupling terms of this kind are not evidence of confinement or of a mass gap in the continuum, which needs $\beta \to \infty$ and asymptotic freedom (the sign of the stored one-loop colour coefficient). The Yang-Mills mass-gap problem is not addressed.

## technical
The strong-coupling expansion of a lattice gauge theory computes its coefficients from averages of products of link variables over the gauge group. In the colour block of the series' algebra, the six vectors $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ with the complex structure $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$, the colour group is the set of rotations commuting with $J$ that fix the real part of the $J$-complex volume trivector; its Lie algebra is the eight $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ bivectors. Inside it the $J$-commuting signed permutations of the six vectors that fix that trivector form a finite group of order 96, each element the action of a rational versor; it is irreducible on the complex three-space, so by Schur's lemma its centre consists of complex scalars, and it has none but $1$. Its averages agree exactly with the colour group's Haar averages for every polynomial of degree at most three in a link, which is shown without importing any Haar integral: in degrees one to three its invariant tensors are exactly those the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ bivectors annihilate (the metric and the form of $J$; the real and imaginary volume trivectors). So every strong-coupling term with each link to degree at most three is the same for both groups: the gluing factor $\tfrac13$, the term $(\beta/18)^{A}$ that a rectangle's own plaquettes contribute to its fundamental Wilson loop with $\beta = 6/g^{2}$ (the leading term for the colour group, by its centre; for the finite group, which has no centre, not shown to be leading), the tube terms of plaquette correlators, and the plaquette average $\beta/18 + \beta^{2}/216$. They first differ in degree four, where the finite group has twenty invariants against twelve, including the fourth power of the complex trace, which the colour group's centre forbids; the plaquette average then differs at $\beta^{3}$. The finite group's weight is gapped at the identity. As a reading (argued): the finite group freezes at weak coupling and has no continuum limit, so, with compact $U(1)$, already stored as sharing the form of the area law and known to be massless at weak coupling, strong-coupling terms of this kind decide neither confinement nor a mass gap in the continuum. Transport-absent.

## lay
A standard way to study the strong nuclear force is to put it on a grid and expand in powers of a small number valid when the force is very strong. This result shows, exactly, that many of the first terms of that expansion are the same for the true symmetry of the strong force and for a finite group of 96 discrete rotations that sits inside it. The finite version behaves very differently when the force is weak: it freezes and has no smooth limit. So these terms cannot tell whether the real force confines quarks or produces a mass gap, which is a famous unsolved problem that this result does not touch.

## one-liner
In the colour block of $\Cl(9,0)$ the $J$-commuting signed permutations of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ fixing the $J$-volume trivector form a finite subgroup of $SU(3)$ of order 96 with trivial centre (Schur) whose averages equal the Haar averages on every link polynomial of degree at most three (derived from invariant tensors) and differ in degree four (a centre-forbidden moment); so every strong-coupling term of link degree at most three is the same for both: the gluing factor $\tfrac13$, the term $(\beta/18)^{A}$ from a rectangle's own plaquettes ($\beta = 6/g^{2}$; leading for $SU(3)$ by its centre, not shown leading for the finite group), the tube terms of plaquette correlators and the plaquette $\beta/18 + \beta^{2}/216$, while the plaquette differs first at $\beta^{3}$ ($0$ against $\tfrac1{972}$); the finite weight is gapped at the identity; as a reading, such terms do not distinguish $SU(3)$ from a group without centre that freezes at weak coupling; the mass-gap problem is not addressed; transport-absent.

proofs.proof-main.tex:
\emph{Conventions.} Lattice weights, Haar measure, the absence of gauge fixing and $\beta = 2N/g^{2}$ ($= 6/g^{2}$ here) are those of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i); the tree gauge and the Haar change of variables are those of the proof of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(iv), (v). The colour factor is the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}, in the colour block of $\Cl(9,0)$ as in the stored field-level BRST result for the derived gauge fields. A bivector $B$ acts on $V$ by $v \mapsto \tfrac12(vB - Bv)$; the check computes with $6 \times 6$ matrices of these actions and of signed permutations, each first matched with the Clifford product.

\emph{Step 1 (the colour group; computed, with a standard reading).} A rotation $U$ of $V$ commuting with $j$ is complex linear for the complex structure $j$ and unitary for the Hermitian form whose real part is the metric, so the group of such rotations is $U(3)$. On the complexified trivectors, $U$ preserves the complex line spanned by the $J$-volume form, and acts on it by its $J$-determinant (or its conjugate, by convention); on the real plane spanned by $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$ this is the rotation by the argument of the determinant. So $U$ fixes $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ exactly when its determinant is $1$, and the group is $SU(3)$, which is connected. The check confirms the convention on $\mathrm{diag}(j, 1, 1)$, of determinant $j$, which turns $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ into $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$. Its Lie algebra consists of the bivectors $B$ of $V$ with $[B, J] = 0$ and $[B, \mathrm{Re}\,\Omega] = 0$ (the derivative of $RXR^{-1}$ along $R = \exp(\epsilon B/2)$ is $\tfrac12[B, X]$); solving these linear conditions on the fifteen bivectors of $V$ gives an eight-dimensional space, closed under the commutator and orthogonal to $J$ in the trace form: $e_{45} - e_{36}$, $e_{35} + e_{46}$, $e_{47} - e_{38}$, $e_{37} + e_{48}$, $e_{56} - e_{34}$, $e_{67} - e_{58}$, $e_{57} + e_{68}$, $e_{78} - e_{34}$. This is (i), first part.

\emph{Step 2 (the finite subgroup; computed).} Let $G$ be generated by the $j$-linear signed permutations with complex matrices $\mathrm{diag}(j, -j, 1)$, $\mathrm{diag}(1, j, -j)$, the cyclic permutation of $e_{3}, e_{5}, e_{7}$ (with $e_{4}, e_{6}, e_{8}$), and the exchange of the first two complex coordinates with the sign of the third reversed. The closure has $96$ elements, the monomial complex matrices with entries in $\{\pm1, \pm j\}$ and determinant $1$. For each element the check builds, by successive reflections, a product $R$ of an even number of vectors with rational components with $RvR^{-1} = g(v)$ on all six basis vectors, and confirms $RJR^{-1} = J$, $R\,\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega\,R^{-1} = \mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $R\,\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega\,R^{-1} = \mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$; so $G \subset SU(3)$. The check solves for the real linear maps of $V$ commuting with the four generators: they form the two-dimensional span of $1$ and $j$. So the only $J$-linear maps commuting with $G$ are the $J$-scalars, $G$ is irreducible on the $J$-complex three-space, and by Schur's lemma every central element of $G$ is a $J$-scalar $a + bj$. Such a signed permutation acts on every complex coordinate by the same unit, so it is one of $\pm1$, $\pm j$, with determinants $1$, $-1$, $\mp j$; so the centre of $G$ is $\{1\}$. The centre of $SU(3)$ consists of the $J$-scalars with $(a + bj)^{3} = 1$, that is $a^{3} - 3ab^{2} = 1$ and $b(3a^{2} - b^{2}) = 0$: either $b = 0$ and $a = 1$, or $b^{2} = 3a^{2}$, whence $-8a^{3} = 1$, $a = -\tfrac12$, $b^{2} = \tfrac34$; so the centre is $1$, $\omega$, $\omega^{2}$, $\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}j$, and $\omega$ has an irrational component (the check confirms that $\tfrac34$ is not the square of a rational). This is (i).

\emph{Step 3 (averages are projectors).} Let $K$ be a compact group with normalised Haar measure acting orthogonally on a real space $W$ (here $W = V^{\otimes k}$, $U \mapsto U^{\otimes k}$), and $P = \int\rho(U)\,dU$. Invariance of the measure gives $\rho(h)P = P = P\rho(h)$, so $P^{2} = P$ and the image of $P$ is the invariant subspace; inversion invariance gives $P^{\mathsf T} = \int\rho(U^{-1})\,dU = P$. So $P$ is the orthogonal projector onto the $K$-invariants, and the same holds for the uniform average over a finite group. A polynomial of degree $k$ in the components of $U$ is a linear functional of $U^{\otimes k}$, so its average is determined by $P$. For $G \subset SU(3)$, the $SU(3)$-invariants are $G$-invariant; conversely, a $G$-invariant tensor annihilated by every element of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ acting as a derivation is invariant under $\exp$ of the algebra, hence under the connected $SU(3)$. So if the $G$-invariants are all annihilated by $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, the two invariant subspaces coincide and the averages agree in that degree.

\emph{Step 4 (degrees one to three; proved with computation).} $G$ acts on the basis tensors of $V^{\otimes k}$ by signed permutations, so its invariants are spanned by the signed orbit sums of the orbits on which no element reverses a tensor's sign; the check finds $0$, $2$ and $2$ such orbits for $k = 1, 2, 3$, identifies the spans with the metric and the form of $J$ ($k = 2$) and with the tensors of $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$ ($k = 3$), and finds that the eight derivations annihilate them. By Step 3 the averages agree in each degree $k \le 3$; the check also compares the $G$-average of $U^{\otimes k}$ entry by entry with the projector on a set of index pairs. For independent links the average of a product factorises (Fubini), and a polynomial of degree at most three in each link is a sum of products of per-link polynomials of degree at most three, so its averages agree as well. This is (ii).

\emph{Step 5 (degree four; computed).} For $k = 4$ the check finds $20$ signed orbits for $G$ and a $12$-dimensional subspace of their span annihilated by $\mathfrak{su}(3)$; so the invariant spaces differ, and $\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{4}dU = \mathrm{tr}\,P = 12$ against $20$ for $G$ (also by summing over $G$). The derivation $D$ of $j$ commutes with $G$; it vanishes on the $12$ colour invariants, and on the $20$ invariants of $G$ its kernel has dimension $18$ and the kernel of $D^{2} + 16$ dimension $2$. On the complexification, $D$ is $j(p - q)$ on the tensors with $p$ factors from the $+j$ eigenspace and $q$ from the $-j$ eigenspace, and $\omega = \exp(2\pi J/3)$ acts there by $\omega^{p - q}$; so the two extra directions with $D^{2} = -16$ have $p - q = \pm4$, on which $\omega$ acts by $\omega^{\pm1} \neq 1$. Concretely, the $J$-complex trace $t = \sum_{k}(U_{2k,2k} + jU_{2k+1,2k})$ has $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}t^{4} = 1$ and $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}|t|^{4} = 3$ (computed), while for $SU(3)$ the substitution $U \mapsto \omega U$ preserves $dU$ and multiplies $t^{4}$ by $\omega^{4} = \omega$, so $\int t^{4}\,dU = 0$. This is (iii).

\emph{Step 6 (shared strong-coupling data; proved).} The gluing integrals are polynomials of degree one and two in $U$, so by Step 4 they may be computed over $G$; the check does so on the eighteen basis maps $E_{kl}$, $jE_{kl}$ of the $j$-linear maps (complete by bilinearity) and finds $0$ and $\tfrac13\mathrm{tr}(XY)$. Expanding the weight, the strong-coupling expansion of $\langle O\rangle$ for a gauge-invariant polynomial observable $O$ is a ratio of sums of integrals $\int O\prod_{p}\chi(U_{p})^{n_{p}}/n_{p}!$ over finitely many links, and each such integral with degree at most three in each link agrees by Step 4. For the rectangle, fix the tree of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(v) to $1$ (the Haar measure, and the average over $G$, are invariant under the change of variables): the plaquettes become $V_{x+1,y}V_{x,y}^{-1}$ and the loop the product of the right-hand column; integrating the columns one at a time with the gluing rule gives, at each of the $A = RT$ integrations, a factor $\tfrac13$ and a weight $\tfrac{\beta}{6}$, and the last trace $\tfrac16\mathrm{tr}\,1 = 1$, so the term is $(\tfrac{\beta}{6}\cdot\tfrac13)^{A} = (\beta/18)^{A}$. Every link of the rectangle occurs in two factors, degree two, so the same holds for $G$; the check sums over $G$ in the tree gauge for the $1 \times 1$ loop ($\tfrac{1}{18}$) and the $2 \times 1$ loop ($\tfrac{1}{324}$). A tube of plaquettes joining two plaquettes, each to first order, also has every link in exactly two factors. So the term from the rectangle's own plaquettes is shared. Whether it is the leading term for $G$ is not decided here: for $SU(3)$ the centre excludes every lower term, but $G$ has no centre, and by Step 5 it has the degree-four invariant $t^{4}$, which lets a fundamental line end on sheets (four fundamental indices fusing to a $G$-invariant at a link), so surfaces whose plaquette count grows with the perimeter can contribute to $G$'s loops where $SU(3)$'s vanish; for large rectangles such terms may lie below order $\beta^{A}$ (argued, not computed here). This is (iv).

\emph{Step 7 (the plaquette; proved).} With $m_{k}$ the moments of $\chi$, $m_{k} = 6^{-k}\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{k}dU = 6^{-k}$ times the dimension of the invariants of $V^{\otimes k}$ (the trace of the projector, as $\mathrm{tr}(U^{\otimes k}) = (\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{k}$). For $SU(3)$: $m_{1} = 0$, $m_{2} = \tfrac{2}{36} = \tfrac1{18}$, $m_{3} = \tfrac{2}{216} = \tfrac1{108}$, $m_{4} = \tfrac{12}{1296} = \tfrac1{108}$; for $G$ the same except $m_{4} = \tfrac{20}{1296} = \tfrac{5}{324}$ (also by summing $\chi^{k}$ over $G$). The cumulants are $\kappa_{2} = m_{2}$, $\kappa_{3} = m_{3}$, $\kappa_{4} = m_{4} - 3m_{2}^{2}$, which is $0$ for $SU(3)$ and $\tfrac{1}{162}$ for $G$, and $(\ln z)' = \sum_{n}\kappa_{n+1}\beta^{n}/n!$ gives the two series; the check also expands the ratio $\int\chi e^{\beta\chi}/\int e^{\beta\chi}$ over $G$ directly. On the lattice, the character expansion $e^{\beta\chi} = z(\beta)\bigl(1 + \sum_{r \neq 1}d_{r}a_{r}(\beta)\chi_{r}\bigr)$ with $a_{r} = O(\beta)$ holds for any compact group; a product of non-trivial characters integrates to zero unless every link of its plaquettes lies in at least two of them (Schur, $\int\chi_{r}(XU)\,dU = 0$), and the smallest such set in dimension at least three is the boundary of an elementary cube, six plaquettes (standard, as in Drouffe and Zuber's account, cited from memory). So $\ln Z$ is the number of plaquettes times $\ln z$ plus terms of order $\beta^{6}$, and $\langle\chi(U_{p})\rangle = (\ln z)' + O(\beta^{5})$. This is (v).

\emph{Step 8 (the gap at the identity; computed).} The check takes the maximum of $\chi$ over the $95$ elements $g \neq 1$ of $G$: $\tfrac13$ (for instance at $\mathrm{diag}(j, -j, 1)$, real trace $2$).
